title: Containerisation and Orchestration with Docker and Kubernetes
subtitle: Package Python services as lean, secure container images, run multi-container apps with Docker Compose, and deploy, scale and troubleshoot them on Kubernetes.
outcomes: Write optimised, multi-stage Dockerfiles that package Python services as small images running as a non-root user
Run and debug multi-container applications with Docker Compose, using networks, volumes and healthchecks
Explain Kubernetes' architecture and its core objects: Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Services and namespaces
Deploy and scale applications with declarative manifests, probes, ConfigMaps, Secrets and the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
Troubleshoot and manage cluster resources with kubectl, Ingress, resource quotas and limits
prerequisites: Comfort with the Linux command line and basic Python, as Python Scripting and Linux for DevOps teaches them (Linux Command Line Essentials covers the shell). You need a computer with at least 8 GB of memory and Docker (Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows, Docker Engine on Linux), plus kind, kubectl and Helm. No cloud account is needed.
description:
Containers changed how software is shipped: an image carries an application with everything it needs, and Kubernetes runs those images across a cluster of machines, restarting, scaling and updating them for you. This advanced course takes one realistic service, a FastAPI inventory API with a Redis cache, from a first Dockerfile to a highly available deployment on a Kubernetes cluster on your own laptop. You'll see how containers isolate processes with namespaces and cgroups, write lean multi-stage Dockerfiles that run as a non-root user, and run the API and Redis together with Docker Compose, using healthchecks, networks and volumes.

Then you'll move to Kubernetes with kind: the control plane and nodes, Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Services, namespaces and persistent storage. You'll deploy from declarative manifests with startup, readiness and liveness probes, configuration in ConfigMaps and Secrets, rolling updates and rollbacks, and scale on CPU with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler. The last module is about running a cluster day to day: kubectl for diagnosis, the common failure states and their fixes, Ingress and Gateway API, quotas and limits, and keeping services up while nodes are drained. Every module ends with a hands-on lab on your own machine, and the capstone brings it together: a Compose setup for developers and Kubernetes manifests that keep serving while you take nodes away.

modules.title: Introduction to Containerisation
modules.summary: How containers differ from virtual machines, how Docker's client, daemon, images and registries fit together, and the container lifecycle, ending with a first Dockerfile for the course's sample service.

lessons.title: From virtual machines to containers
objectives: Explain how a container differs from a virtual machine
Describe the Linux kernel features that isolate a container
key_points: A virtual machine runs a complete guest operating system, with its own kernel, on virtual hardware provided by a hypervisor. A container is a group of ordinary processes on the host that share the host's kernel.

Isolation comes from two Linux kernel features: namespaces give a container its own view of process IDs, network interfaces, mounts and hostname, and control groups (cgroups) limit and account for the CPU, memory and I/O it can use.

With no guest operating system to boot, a container starts in about the time its own process takes to start and uses far less memory and disk than a VM, so one machine can run many more containers than VMs.

Sharing the kernel is the trade-off: a container can't bring its own kernel, Linux containers need a Linux kernel (Docker Desktop runs one in a small VM on macOS and Windows), and a kernel flaw affects every container on the host, so VMs isolate more strongly.

An image packages the application with its exact runtime and libraries, so it behaves the same on a laptop, in CI and in production; what differs between environments, such as addresses and credentials, is passed in when the container starts.

walkthrough.title: See a container's isolation for yourself

steps.do: Run ps in a throwaway Alpine container. It sees only its own processes, because it has its own PID namespace.
steps.code: docker run --rm alpine:3.22 ps
steps.see: One process, ps itself, as PID 1.

steps.do: Give a container its own hostname: the UTS namespace keeps it separate from the host's.
steps.code: docker run --rm --hostname demo alpine:3.22 hostname
steps.see: demo

steps.do: Compare kernels. A container has no kernel of its own.
steps.code:
uname -r
docker run --rm alpine:3.22 uname -r
steps.see: On Linux, the same version twice. On macOS and Windows, the container reports the kernel of Docker Desktop's Linux VM, not your computer's.

steps.do: Set a memory limit and read it back from the container's cgroup: 64 MB is 67108864 bytes.
steps.code: docker run --rm --memory 64m alpine:3.22 cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max
steps.see: 67108864, on hosts that use cgroup v2, as current Linux distributions and Docker Desktop do.

lessons.title: Docker's architecture: client, daemon, images and registries
objectives: Describe how the Docker client, daemon and container runtime work together
Explain the difference between an image, a container and a registry
key_points: The docker command is a client: it sends API requests to the Docker daemon (dockerd), which builds images and manages containers, handing the low-level work to containerd and runc, the OCI runtime that sets up each container's namespaces and cgroups.

An image is a read-only template: a stack of filesystem layers plus metadata such as the default command, environment variables and exposed ports. A container is an instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top, which is lost when the container is removed.

Images are kept in registries such as Docker Hub or a private registry. A reference like docker.io/library/python:3.13-slim names the registry, repository and tag; a tag can be moved to a new image, but a digest (@sha256:...) always names the same one.
Images and runtimes follow the Open Container Initiative (OCI) specifications, so an image built with Docker also runs under containerd, CRI-O or Podman, which is how Kubernetes nodes run it.
Pin base images to a specific version tag, or a digest, rather than latest, so a rebuild next month gives the same result and updates happen when you choose.

walkthrough.title: Inspect an image and its layers

steps.do: Pull the slim Python image and list the Python images you have.
steps.code:
docker pull python:3.13-slim-trixie
docker image ls python

steps.do: Show which platform the image was built for.
steps.code: docker image inspect python:3.13-slim-trixie --format '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}'
steps.see: linux/amd64 or linux/arm64, matching your machine.

steps.do: See its layers and the instructions that made them.
steps.code: docker history python:3.13-slim-trixie
steps.see: One line per instruction, newest first, with the size each one added.

steps.do: Find the digest that names this exact image.
steps.code: docker image inspect python:3.13-slim-trixie --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}'
steps.see: python@sha256: followed by 64 hexadecimal characters.

steps.do: See what the daemon is looking after.
steps.code: docker system df
steps.see: The space used by images, containers, local volumes and the build cache.

lessons.title: The container lifecycle and your first Dockerfile
objectives: Run, inspect, stop and remove containers
Write a Dockerfile that packages a Python web service
key_points: docker run creates and starts a container, which runs for as long as its main process (PID 1) runs. -d runs it in the background, --name names it, -e sets an environment variable and --rm removes it when it exits.

docker ps lists running containers (-a adds stopped ones), docker logs shows what the main process wrote to standard output and standard error, and docker exec runs another command inside a running container.
docker stop sends SIGTERM and, if the process hasn't exited after a grace period (10 seconds by default), SIGKILL; docker rm deletes a stopped container along with its writable layer.

In a Dockerfile, FROM chooses the base image, WORKDIR sets the working folder, COPY adds files from the build context, RUN runs a command at build time, ENV sets variables, EXPOSE documents a port and CMD sets the default command.

Write CMD in exec form, a JSON array such as ["uvicorn", "app.main:app"], so your app is PID 1 and gets SIGTERM directly. The shell form starts it through /bin/sh -c, where it may never see the signal, so docker stop waits out the grace period and kills it.

-p 8000:8000 publishes container port 8000 on the host, and the app must listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container, because 127.0.0.1 there is unreachable from outside. A .dockerignore file keeps .git, virtual environments and secrets out of the build context.

lab.title: Run containers and package the inventory API
lab.goal: Practise the container lifecycle, then package the course's sample service, inventory-api (a FastAPI app that caches lookups in Redis), with a first Dockerfile, and see how it behaves when its cache is missing.
setup: Docker Desktop (macOS or Windows) or Docker Engine (Linux), running
A terminal with curl, which macOS, Linux and Windows 10 and later include
Download the starter files into a folder called inventory-api

steps.do: Check that the client can reach the daemon, and run the hello-world image.
steps.code:
docker version
docker run --rm hello-world
steps.see: Client and Server sections, then a message that starts Hello from Docker!

steps.do: Start Redis in the background, then look at it from outside: list it, read its log and run a command in it.
steps.code:
docker run -d --name demo redis:8.2-alpine
docker ps
docker logs demo | tail -n 3
docker exec demo redis-cli ping
steps.see: demo in the list, Ready to accept connections in the log, and PONG.

steps.do: Stop it, find it among all containers, then remove it.
steps.code:
docker stop demo
docker ps -a --filter name=demo
docker rm demo
steps.see: A STATUS starting with Exited before you remove it.

steps.do: In the inventory-api folder, create a file named .dockerignore, so the build context leaves out what the image doesn't need.
steps.code:
.git/
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env
k8s/

steps.do: Create a file named Dockerfile with this first, simple version. It builds on the full Python image; module 2 slims it down.
steps.code:
FROM python:3.13-trixie
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY app/ ./app/
ENV APP_VERSION=1.0.0
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

steps.do: Build the image and list it.
steps.code:
docker build -t inventory-api:1.0.0 .
docker image ls inventory-api
steps.see: inventory-api 1.0.0 and its size: note the size for module 2.

steps.do: Run it with port 8000 published, and call it.
steps.code:
docker run -d --name inv -p 8000:8000 inventory-api:1.0.0
curl -s localhost:8000/
curl -s localhost:8000/healthz
steps.see: {"service":"inventory-api","version":"1.0.0","host":"..."} and {"status":"ok"}

steps.do: Ask whether it's ready. There's no Redis for it to use, so readiness says no, while the service still answers, just without its cache.
steps.code:
curl -s -i localhost:8000/readyz
curl -s localhost:8000/items/sku-1001
steps.see: HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable with {"status":"waiting for redis"}, then the item with "cache":"miss".

steps.do: Compare the container's hostname with the host field above, and check how the image starts.
steps.code:
docker exec inv hostname
docker image inspect inventory-api:1.0.0 --format '{{json .Config.Cmd}}'
steps.see: The container ID, then ["uvicorn","app.main:app","--host","0.0.0.0","--port","8000"]

steps.do: Read the container's log, then stop and remove it in one command.
steps.code:
docker logs inv
docker rm -f inv
steps.see: uvicorn's access log, one line for each request you made.

checks.text: Docker works, and the lifecycle commands ran against the Redis container.
The image builds and the service answers on port 8000 as version 1.0.0.
Without Redis, readiness answers 503 while liveness still passes.
The image's default command is in exec form.

lab.submit: Paste your Dockerfile, then the commands and output from steps 1, 2, 6, 7, 8 and 9.

files.content: """inventory-api: the sample service for this course."""

fastapi==0.146.0
uvicorn==0.54.0
redis==8.1.0

hints: If docker version shows no Server section, the daemon isn't running: start Docker Desktop, or run sudo systemctl start docker on Linux.
Bind for 0.0.0.0:8000 failed means another program uses port 8000: stop it, or publish a different host port with -p 8080:8000 and call localhost:8080.
A connection reset straight after docker run means the app is still starting: wait a second and try again, or read docker logs inv.
In Windows PowerShell, curl can be an alias for Invoke-WebRequest: type curl.exe, or use Git Bash or WSL.

modules.title: Docker and Docker Compose
modules.summary: Write efficient, secure Dockerfiles with layer caching and multi-stage builds, manage images responsibly, and run multi-container applications with Docker Compose, its networks and its volumes.

lessons.title: Efficient Dockerfiles: layers, caching and multi-stage builds
objectives: Order Dockerfile instructions to make the most of the build cache
Use a multi-stage build to produce a small runtime image
key_points: Each RUN, COPY and ADD instruction creates a layer. Docker reuses a cached layer when the instruction and its inputs haven't changed, and rebuilds every layer after the first one that has.
Order instructions from least to most often changed: copy requirements.txt and install the dependencies before copying the source code, so editing code doesn't reinstall every package.

A multi-stage build has several FROM stages. Compilers, headers and caches stay in an early build stage, COPY --from=build copies only the result, such as a virtual environment, into a slim runtime stage, and only the last stage becomes the image.

Keep the stages on the same Python version and Debian release, such as python:3.13-trixie and python:3.13-slim-trixie: a virtual environment points at its interpreter's path, and compiled packages need the same system libraries.

A file deleted in a later layer still takes up space in the layer that added it, so clean up in the same RUN instruction, or leave the mess in a build stage. A BuildKit cache mount (RUN --mount=type=cache) speeds up rebuilds without putting pip's cache in the image.

walkthrough.title: Watch the build cache at work

steps.do: In your inventory-api folder, build the image twice. The second build takes a moment, because every step is reused.
steps.code:
docker build -t inventory-api:cache-test .
docker build -t inventory-api:cache-test .
steps.see: CACHED beside each step of the second build.

steps.do: Change only the code by appending a comment to app/main.py, and build again.
steps.code:
echo '# cache test' >> app/main.py
docker build -t inventory-api:cache-test .
steps.see: The pip install step is still CACHED; only COPY app/ and the steps after it run.

steps.do: Now add a blank line to requirements.txt and build again.
steps.code:
echo '' >> requirements.txt
docker build -t inventory-api:cache-test .
steps.see: The install step runs again, because one of its inputs changed.

steps.do: Remove the comment and the blank line you added, then delete the test image.
steps.code: docker image rm inventory-api:cache-test

lessons.title: Image hygiene: tags, users, secrets and scanning
objectives: Tag and version images so deployments are repeatable
Harden an image with a non-root user, no secrets and fewer vulnerabilities
key_points: Tag every build with an immutable version, such as inventory-api:1.1.0 or the Git commit SHA, and never push different contents under a version already used; latest is just the default tag name, not a promise of the newest build.

Containers run as root unless the image or the runtime says otherwise. Create a user in the Dockerfile and switch to it with USER, ideally by numeric UID such as 10001, so Kubernetes can verify runAsNonRoot and a compromised process has less power.

Never put secrets in an image: every layer can be read back, including files deleted in a later layer and values passed with --build-arg. Supply secrets when the container runs, or use a BuildKit secret mount (RUN --mount=type=secret) for build-time credentials.

Scan images for known vulnerabilities in operating-system packages and libraries with a scanner such as Docker Scout, Trivy or Grype, rebuild regularly to pick up patched base images, and keep images small so there's less to patch.
Docker's HEALTHCHECK instruction lets Docker and Compose mark a container healthy or unhealthy; Kubernetes ignores it and uses its own probes instead.
docker system df shows the space taken by images, containers, volumes and the build cache, and docker image prune removes dangling images, the untagged leftovers of rebuilds.

lessons.title: Multi-container apps with Docker Compose
objectives: Describe a multi-container application in a compose.yaml file
Connect services through networks and keep their data in volumes
key_points: Docker Compose describes a whole application in compose.yaml: its services, networks and volumes. docker compose up -d builds or pulls the images and starts everything; docker compose down stops and removes the containers and networks.

Compose creates a network for the project, and each service reaches the others by service name through Docker's built-in DNS, so the API connects to Redis at cache:6379; containers that aren't on that network can't reach it at all.

A container's writable layer goes when the container goes, so data that must last lives in a volume: a named volume managed by Docker for databases, or a bind mount of a host folder for code during development. docker compose down keeps named volumes unless you add -v.
depends_on only orders start-up. With condition: service_healthy, Compose waits for the dependency's healthcheck to pass first, so the API doesn't start before Redis accepts connections.

Environment variables, .env files and profiles let one file serve several uses, but Compose runs everything on one host: it doesn't spread containers across machines, move them when a machine fails or scale them on load. That's what Kubernetes adds.

steps.do: Check the file: Compose prints the fully resolved configuration, or the first error it finds.
steps.code: docker compose config

steps.do: Start the stack in the background, rebuilding images whose files changed, and wait until it's healthy.
steps.code: docker compose up -d --build --wait

steps.do: See each service's state, then follow the API's log (Ctrl+C stops following, not the service).
steps.code:
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f api
steps.see: STATUS shows (healthy) once a service's healthcheck passes.

steps.do: Run a command inside a service's container.
steps.code: docker compose exec cache redis-cli dbsize

steps.do: Stop and remove the containers and network; add -v to delete the named volumes too.
steps.code: docker compose down

lab.title: Slim the image and run the stack with Compose
lab.goal: Rebuild inventory-api as a multi-stage image that runs as a non-root user, then run it with Redis under Docker Compose, with healthchecks, a private network and a volume that keeps data across restarts.
setup: Your inventory-api folder from the module 1 lab, with the image inventory-api:1.0.0
Docker with Compose v2: docker compose version should print a version

steps.do: Rename your module 1 Dockerfile to Dockerfile.single, and write a new Dockerfile with a build stage and a runtime stage.
steps.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# Build stage: the full Python image, with compilers in case a package needs building.
FROM python:3.13-trixie AS build
WORKDIR /build
RUN python -m venv /opt/venv
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt

# Runtime stage: the slim image of the same Python and Debian release, plus the venv and the code.
FROM python:3.13-slim-trixie AS runtime
ARG APP_VERSION=1.1.0
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH" \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    APP_VERSION=${APP_VERSION}
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --no-create-home appuser
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /opt/venv /opt/venv
COPY app/ ./app/
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=10s --timeout=3s --start-period=5s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz', timeout=2)"]
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

steps.do: Build version 1.1.0 and compare the two images.
steps.code:
docker build -t inventory-api:1.1.0 .
docker image ls inventory-api
steps.see: Both tags: 1.1.0, built on the slim image, is several times smaller than 1.0.0.

steps.do: Check which user the container runs as, and look through the runtime image's layers.
steps.code:
docker run --rm inventory-api:1.1.0 id
docker history inventory-api:1.1.0
steps.see: uid=10001(appuser), and no compilers or pip cache among the layers.

steps.do: Create compose.yaml next to the Dockerfile.
steps.code:
name: inventory

services:
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      args:
        APP_VERSION: "1.1.0"
    image: inventory-api:1.1.0
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: cache
      CACHE_TTL_SECONDS: "30"
    depends_on:
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - backend
    restart: unless-stopped

  cache:
    image: redis:8.2-alpine
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
    volumes:
      - cache-data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
    networks:
      - backend

volumes:
  cache-data:

networks:
  backend:

steps.do: Validate the file, start the stack, and wait until both services are healthy.
steps.code:
docker compose config --quiet && echo valid
docker compose up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
steps.see: valid, then both services with (healthy) in their STATUS.

steps.do: Look up an item twice: the first lookup is slow and fills the cache, the second comes from Redis.
steps.code:
curl -s localhost:8000/items/sku-1001
curl -s localhost:8000/items/sku-1001
steps.see: "cache":"miss", then "cache":"hit"

steps.do: Record three visits, remove and recreate the containers, then record one more. The total survives because Redis keeps its data in the cache-data volume.
steps.code:
for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/visits; echo; done
docker compose down
docker compose up -d --wait
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/visits
steps.see: "visits":1 to "visits":3, then "visits":4 after the restart.

steps.do: Prove the network is private: a container on the project's network reaches cache, one on Docker's default network can't even resolve the name.
steps.code:
docker run --rm --network inventory_backend redis:8.2-alpine redis-cli -h cache ping
docker run --rm redis:8.2-alpine redis-cli -h cache ping
steps.see: PONG, then Could not connect to Redis at cache:6379 and the reason.

steps.do: Read the API's last log lines, then clean up, deleting the volume too.
steps.code:
docker compose logs api --tail 5
docker compose down -v

checks.text: The multi-stage image builds and runs as the non-root user.
Compose reports both services healthy.
The second lookup is served from the Redis cache.
The visit count survives recreating the containers, because it lives in the volume.
Only containers on the project's network can reach Redis.

lab.submit: Paste your Dockerfile and compose.yaml, the docker image ls output, and the commands and output from steps 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8.
hints: If the build fails at RUN --mount, BuildKit is off: it's the default in Docker Desktop and Docker Engine 23 and later; on older engines set DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1.
If the network in step 8 isn't found, run docker network ls: its name is the project name from compose.yaml (inventory) followed by _backend.
If api never becomes healthy, read docker compose logs api: a typo in app.main:app or a missing app/__init__.py stops uvicorn starting.
If the second lookup is also a miss, the API can't reach Redis: REDIS_HOST must be the service name, cache, not localhost.

modules.title: Kubernetes Primitives
modules.summary: How a Kubernetes cluster is built, and the objects you use every day: Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Services, namespaces and persistent storage, explored on a three-node kind cluster.

lessons.title: Kubernetes architecture: the control plane and the nodes
objectives: Describe what each control-plane and node component does
Explain how Kubernetes reconciles desired and actual state
key_points: A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane, which decides what should run, and worker nodes, which run it. You declare the desired state as objects, and controllers keep working to make the actual state match it.

The API server (kube-apiserver) is the only way in: kubectl, controllers and nodes all read and write objects through it, and it stores them in etcd, a consistent key-value store that holds the whole cluster's state.

The scheduler (kube-scheduler) chooses a node for each new Pod, one with enough unreserved CPU and memory that meets the Pod's constraints, while kube-controller-manager runs the reconciliation loops that, for example, replace missing Pods.

On every node, the kubelet starts the Pods assigned to it through a container runtime such as containerd and reports their status; kube-proxy routes Service traffic, and a CNI plugin gives every Pod an IP address on one flat cluster network.

kind (Kubernetes in Docker) runs each node as a Docker container, and minikube runs a cluster in a VM or a container: both give you a real cluster on a laptop for learning and testing, not for production.

steps.do: Create a single-node cluster called tour, and check that kubectl can reach it.
steps.code:
kind create cluster --name tour
kubectl cluster-info --context kind-tour
steps.see: Kubernetes control plane is running at https://127.0.0.1:... and the CoreDNS address.

steps.do: List the nodes, then the control-plane components, which run as Pods in the kube-system namespace.
steps.code:
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
steps.see: etcd, kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler Pods named after tour-control-plane, plus coredns, kube-proxy and kindnet, kind's CNI plugin.

steps.do: See every kind of object the API server serves, with its API group.
steps.code: kubectl api-resources | head -n 25

steps.do: Each kind node is a Docker container: find this one.
steps.code: docker ps --filter name=tour
steps.see: One container, tour-control-plane, running a kindest/node image.

steps.do: Delete the cluster.
steps.code: kind delete cluster --name tour

lessons.title: Pods, ReplicaSets and Deployments
objectives: Explain why Pods are created by controllers rather than directly
Describe how a Deployment rolls out a new version through ReplicaSets
key_points: A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that share a network namespace (one IP address, so they talk over localhost) and can share volumes. Most Pods have one main container, with helpers beside it only when they must be.
Pods are disposable. If a bare Pod is deleted or its node fails, nothing recreates it, so you rarely create Pods yourself: a controller creates them from a Pod template.

A ReplicaSet keeps a set number of identical Pods running, counting the Pods that match its label selector. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets for you, and is what you normally write for a stateless service.

Changing a Deployment's Pod template, such as its image, starts a rolling update: a new ReplicaSet scales up as the old one scales down, within maxSurge and maxUnavailable, and kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous ReplicaSet.
Labels are key-value pairs on objects, and selectors choose objects by label. A Deployment's selector must match its Pod template's labels, and can't be changed after the Deployment is created.

lessons.title: Services, DNS and namespaces
objectives: Choose the right Service type for a workload
Reach a Service by its DNS name from another namespace
key_points: Pod IP addresses change whenever Pods are replaced, so a Service gives the Pods matching its selector one stable virtual IP address and DNS name, and spreads connections across those that are ready.

A ClusterIP Service, the default, is reachable only inside the cluster; NodePort also opens a port (30000 to 32767 by default) on every node; LoadBalancer asks the cloud for an external load balancer; a headless Service (clusterIP: None) returns the Pods' own addresses.
The cluster DNS server, CoreDNS, gives every Service a name: inventory-api from Pods in the same namespace, and inventory-api.shop.svc.cluster.local (or inventory-api.shop) from any namespace.
Kubernetes lists the ready Pods behind a Service in EndpointSlices. A Service with no endpoints nearly always means its selector doesn't match the Pods' labels, or none of the matching Pods is ready.

Namespaces divide a cluster into groups of objects: names only need to be unique within one, and quotas and access rules apply per namespace. Nodes, PersistentVolumes and namespaces themselves belong to none, and a namespace alone isn't a security boundary.

lessons.title: Volumes, persistent storage and StatefulSets
objectives: Choose between emptyDir, ConfigMap, Secret and persistent volumes
Explain when to use a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment
key_points: A container's files are lost when it restarts, so Pods declare volumes: an emptyDir lasts as long as the Pod (scratch space, or files shared between its containers), and ConfigMap and Secret volumes present configuration as files.

For data that must outlive any Pod, a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) asks for storage of a size and access mode; a StorageClass's provisioner creates a matching PersistentVolume (PV) on demand, and the Pod mounts the claim by name.

Access modes say how a volume can be mounted: ReadWriteOnce by one node at a time (most block storage, and kind's default local-path class), ReadWriteOncePod by a single Pod, ReadOnlyMany by many nodes read-only, and ReadWriteMany by many nodes read-write.

A StatefulSet gives each Pod a stable name (redis-0, redis-1), a stable DNS name through a headless Service, and its own PVC from volumeClaimTemplates that stays with it when it's rescheduled. Use it for databases and other stateful software.
A ReadWriteOnce volume ties its Pod to the nodes that can attach it, and with kind's local-path class that's one particular node, so drain that node and the Pod has nowhere to go until it returns.

lab.title: Explore Kubernetes primitives on kind
lab.goal: Create a three-node kind cluster, load the inventory-api image into it, and see Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Services and namespaces at work, including why a Deployment's Pod comes back and a bare Pod doesn't.
setup: Docker running, with the inventory-api:1.1.0 image from the module 2 lab
kind and kubectl installed: kind version and kubectl version --client should both answer
Download the starter files: kind-config.yaml, pod.yaml, deployment.yaml and service.yaml

steps.do: Create the cluster from the config: one control-plane node and two workers, with port 30080 mapped to your computer for later labs.
steps.code:
kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml
kubectl get nodes
steps.see: Set kubectl context to "kind-lab", then lab-control-plane, lab-worker and lab-worker2, all Ready.

steps.do: List the control-plane components and where they run.
steps.code: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide
steps.see: etcd-lab-control-plane, kube-apiserver-lab-control-plane, kube-controller-manager-lab-control-plane and kube-scheduler-lab-control-plane, plus coredns, kindnet and kube-proxy Pods.

steps.do: The cluster's nodes can't see the images on your computer, so load yours into them.
steps.code: kind load docker-image inventory-api:1.1.0 --name lab

steps.do: Create a bare Pod, see which node it landed on, then delete it. Nothing brings it back.
steps.code:
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
kubectl get pod inventory-pod -o wide
kubectl delete pod inventory-pod
kubectl get pods
steps.see: No resources found in default namespace. after the delete.

steps.do: Create the Deployment and list the objects it manages.
steps.code:
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get deployment,replicaset,pods -l app=inventory-api -o wide
steps.see: The Deployment at 3/3, one ReplicaSet with 3 ready, and three Pods spread over the workers.

steps.do: Delete one of the Deployment's Pods and watch the ReplicaSet replace it.
steps.code:
kubectl delete pod $(kubectl get pods -l app=inventory-api -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl get pods -l app=inventory-api
steps.see: Three Pods again, one of them only seconds old.

steps.do: Create the Service and look at the endpoints behind it.
steps.code:
kubectl apply -f service.yaml
kubectl get service inventory-api
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=inventory-api
steps.see: A ClusterIP Service on port 80, and an EndpointSlice with three Pod addresses on port 8000.

steps.do: Call the Service from inside the cluster with a temporary Pod. Run it a few times: different Pods answer.
steps.code: kubectl run curl --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.17.0 -- curl -s http://inventory-api/
steps.see: {"service":"inventory-api","version":"1.1.0","host":"inventory-api-..."}, then a line saying the curl Pod was deleted.

steps.do: Scale the Deployment out, then back.
steps.code:
kubectl scale deployment inventory-api --replicas=5
kubectl get deployment inventory-api
kubectl scale deployment inventory-api --replicas=3
steps.see: 5/5 once the new Pods are ready.

steps.do: Create a namespace, and call the Service from it by its full DNS name.
steps.code:
kubectl create namespace sandbox
kubectl run curl -n sandbox --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.17.0 -- curl -s http://inventory-api.default.svc.cluster.local/
kubectl get pods -n sandbox
steps.see: The same kind of answer, then No resources found in sandbox namespace.

checks.text: The three-node cluster is running, with its control-plane components.
The bare Pod isn't recreated after it's deleted.
look_for: No resources found in default namespace

checks.text: The Deployment keeps three replicas and replaces a deleted Pod.
The Service has endpoints and answers inside the cluster, including from another namespace by its full DNS name.

lab.submit: Paste the commands and output from steps 1, 2 and 4 to 8 and step 10, then two sentences explaining why the bare Pod stayed deleted while the Deployment's Pod came back.

files.content:
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
name: lab
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    extraPortMappings:
      - containerPort: 30080   # a NodePort, reachable on the host as localhost:30080
        hostPort: 30080
        protocol: TCP
  - role: worker
  - role: worker

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: inventory-pod
  labels:
    app: inventory-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: inventory-api:1.1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8000

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: inventory-api
  labels:
    app: inventory-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: inventory-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: inventory-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: inventory-api:1.1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service

  name: inventory-api
spec:
  selector:
    app: inventory-api
  ports:
    - port: 80

hints: ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff means the nodes don't have the image: run kind load docker-image again, and check the tag matches the manifest exactly.
If kind can't create the cluster because port 30080 is taken, free it or change hostPort in kind-config.yaml, and use that port in later labs.
kubectl talks to the cluster its current context names: kubectl config current-context should print kind-lab.
If Pods stay Pending, give Docker more memory: at least 6 GB in Docker Desktop's Resources settings.

modules.title: Deploying and Scaling on K8s
modules.summary: Deploy an application from declarative manifests, keep traffic away from unhealthy Pods with probes, supply configuration and secrets, update it without downtime, and scale it with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler.

lessons.title: Declarative manifests and kubectl apply
objectives: Write manifests with the correct API version and kind for each object
Apply, preview and validate changes declaratively
key_points: A manifest is a YAML (or JSON) description of objects. Each has apiVersion, kind, metadata (name, namespace, labels) and usually spec, the desired state; Kubernetes fills in status, the state it observes.

Use each object's API group and version: v1 for Pods, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets and Namespaces; apps/v1 for Deployments and StatefulSets; autoscaling/v2 for HorizontalPodAutoscalers; networking.k8s.io/v1 for Ingress; policy/v1 for PodDisruptionBudgets.

kubectl apply -f is declarative: it creates what's missing and changes what differs, so files in Git stay the source of truth. kubectl diff -f shows what would change, and kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f has the API server validate without saving.

kubectl apply -f on a folder applies its files in name order, so number them (00-namespace.yaml first) when one object must exist before another. Keep imperative commands such as kubectl scale and edit for experiments.
Tools build on plain manifests: Kustomize, built into kubectl as apply -k, layers changes for each environment over a shared base, and Helm packages manifests as versioned, templated charts.

walkthrough.title: Generate, check and apply a manifest

steps.do: Read the documentation for a field without leaving the terminal.
steps.code: kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate
steps.see: What maxSurge and maxUnavailable mean, and that both default to 25%.

steps.do: Generate a starting manifest instead of typing it from memory.
steps.code: kubectl create deployment hello --image=inventory-api:1.1.0 --replicas=2 --dry-run=client -o yaml > hello.yaml
steps.see: A complete Deployment in hello.yaml, ready to edit.

steps.do: Have the API server validate it without saving anything.
steps.code: kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f hello.yaml
steps.see: deployment.apps/hello created (server dry run)

steps.do: Apply it, change replicas to 3 in the file, and preview the change before applying it again.
steps.code:
kubectl apply -f hello.yaml
kubectl diff -f hello.yaml
steps.see: A diff in which replicas changes from 2 to 3.

steps.do: Delete everything the file created.
steps.code: kubectl delete -f hello.yaml

lessons.title: Health checks, resources and rolling updates
objectives: Configure startup, readiness and liveness probes for what each is for
Set resource requests and limits, and update a Deployment without downtime
key_points: A readiness probe decides whether a Pod gets traffic: while it fails, the Pod is taken out of its Services' endpoints but keeps running. Check what the Pod needs in order to serve requests, such as its cache connection.

A liveness probe decides whether a container is restarted: after failureThreshold failures in a row, the kubelet kills and restarts it. Keep it cheap and independent of other services, or one slow database restarts every Pod that uses it.
A startup probe holds off the liveness and readiness probes until it succeeds, so a slow-starting container isn't killed while it loads.

Requests are what the scheduler reserves for a container; limits are the most it may use. Going over a CPU limit throttles the container, going over its memory limit gets it killed (OOMKilled), and requests are the basis of the autoscaler's utilisation figures.

With a RollingUpdate strategy of maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0, Kubernetes starts a new Pod, waits until it's ready, then removes an old one, so capacity never drops during an update; readiness probes are what make that safe.

lessons.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets
objectives: Supply configuration to Pods as environment variables or files
Handle Secrets with an understanding of what they do and don't protect
key_points: ConfigMaps hold non-secret configuration and Secrets hold sensitive values; both keep configuration out of the image, so the same image runs unchanged in every environment.

A Pod reads them as environment variables (env with valueFrom, or envFrom for every key) or as files in a volume. Mounted files update a little while after the object changes; environment variables are fixed when the container starts, so restart the Deployment (kubectl rollout restart) to apply them.

Secret values are only base64-encoded, not encrypted: anyone who can read the Secret can decode it. Restrict who can read Secrets with RBAC, turn on encryption at rest for etcd, and never commit real Secret manifests to Git.

In production, secrets usually come from a manager such as HashiCorp Vault or a cloud provider's secret manager, synchronised by a tool such as the External Secrets Operator or mounted by the Secrets Store CSI Driver; Sealed Secrets lets you keep encrypted secrets in Git.
If a Pod refers to a ConfigMap, Secret or key that doesn't exist, its container isn't started and the Pod shows CreateContainerConfigError until the reference can be resolved.

lessons.title: Scaling with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
objectives: Explain how the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decides how many replicas to run
Configure an autoscaler on CPU utilisation, with sensible scaling behaviour
key_points: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (autoscaling/v2) changes a workload's replica count to keep a metric near a target, such as average CPU use at 60% of the Pods' CPU requests.
It needs metrics: CPU and memory come from metrics-server, which kubectl top also reads, while custom and external metrics need an adapter such as the Prometheus Adapter or KEDA.

The desired count is the current count times the current value divided by the target, rounded up and kept between minReplicas and maxReplicas. Pods without CPU requests have no utilisation, so always set requests.
The behavior section controls the pace: by default scale-down waits for a 300-second stabilisation window, so a short dip in load doesn't remove Pods that are needed again a minute later.
When an autoscaler manages a Deployment, leave replicas out of the Deployment's manifest; otherwise each kubectl apply resets the count the autoscaler chose.

lab.title: Deploy, configure and scale the inventory service
lab.goal: Deploy inventory-api and Redis to their own namespace from numbered manifests, with settings in a ConfigMap and the Redis password in a Secret, then see readiness, a configuration change, autoscaling, a rolling update and a rollback at work.
setup: The kind cluster from the module 3 lab, with your kubectl context set to kind-lab
Your inventory-api folder with the multi-stage Dockerfile from module 2
Download the starter files into a folder called k8s inside inventory-api

steps.do: Build version 1.2.0 for the rolling update later, and load both versions into the cluster.
steps.code:
docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.2.0 -t inventory-api:1.2.0 .
kind load docker-image inventory-api:1.1.0 inventory-api:1.2.0 --name lab

steps.do: Create the namespace, then a random Redis password as a Secret, so no password is ever written in a file.
steps.code:
kubectl apply -f k8s/00-namespace.yaml
kubectl -n shop create secret generic redis-auth --from-literal=password="$(python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(16))')"
steps.see: namespace/shop created and secret/redis-auth created

steps.do: Apply the whole folder (in file-name order, which is why the files are numbered) and wait for the API.
steps.code:
kubectl apply -f k8s/
kubectl -n shop rollout status deployment/inventory-api
steps.see: One line per object, then deployment "inventory-api" successfully rolled out

steps.do: Call the service through its NodePort, which kind maps to localhost:30080.
steps.code:
curl -s localhost:30080/
curl -s localhost:30080/items/sku-1001
curl -s localhost:30080/items/sku-1001
steps.see: Version 1.1.0, then "cache":"miss" and "cache":"hit"

steps.do: See readiness at work: stop Redis, and the API Pods stay Running but become 0/1 ready, so the Service sends them nothing. Then bring Redis back.
steps.code:
kubectl -n shop scale deployment redis --replicas=0
sleep 20
kubectl -n shop get pods -l app=inventory-api
kubectl -n shop scale deployment redis --replicas=1
steps.see: READY 0/1, STATUS Running and no restarts: readiness failed, liveness didn't.

steps.do: Change a setting. Environment variables are read when a container starts, so patch the ConfigMap, then restart the Deployment.
steps.code:
kubectl -n shop exec deploy/inventory-api -- env | grep CACHE_TTL
kubectl -n shop patch configmap inventory-config -p '{"data":{"CACHE_TTL_SECONDS":"10"}}'
kubectl -n shop rollout restart deployment/inventory-api
kubectl -n shop rollout status deployment/inventory-api
kubectl -n shop exec deploy/inventory-api -- env | grep CACHE_TTL
steps.see: CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=30 before the restart, CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=10 after it.

steps.do: See that a Secret is only encoded.
steps.code: kubectl -n shop get secret redis-auth -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode; echo
steps.see: The password in plain text: anyone allowed to read Secrets in shop can do the same.

steps.do: Install metrics-server, where the autoscaler gets CPU figures. kind's kubelets use self-signed certificates, hence the extra argument.
steps.code:
helm repo add metrics-server https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/metrics-server/
helm upgrade --install metrics-server metrics-server/metrics-server -n kube-system --set 'args={--kubelet-insecure-tls}'
kubectl top pods -n shop
steps.see: CPU and memory for each Pod; if metrics aren't available yet, wait a minute and try again.

steps.do: Generate CPU load from inside the cluster and watch the autoscaler scale out (Ctrl+C stops watching).
steps.code:
kubectl -n shop run load --image=busybox:1.37 --restart=Never -- /bin/sh -c 'while true; do wget -q -O /dev/null http://inventory-api/work?ms=200; done'
kubectl -n shop get hpa inventory-api --watch
steps.see: The CPU figure climbs far above the 60% target and REPLICAS rises from 2 towards 6.

steps.do: Stop the load and watch it scale back in after the 60-second stabilisation window set in 50-hpa.yaml.
steps.code:
kubectl -n shop delete pod load
kubectl -n shop get hpa inventory-api --watch
steps.see: REPLICAS returns to 2 within a few minutes.

steps.do: Roll out version 1.2.0 and check it, then roll back.
steps.code:
kubectl -n shop set image deployment/inventory-api api=inventory-api:1.2.0
kubectl -n shop rollout status deployment/inventory-api
curl -s localhost:30080/
kubectl -n shop rollout history deployment/inventory-api
kubectl -n shop rollout undo deployment/inventory-api
kubectl -n shop rollout status deployment/inventory-api
curl -s localhost:30080/
steps.see: "version":"1.2.0", then deployment.apps/inventory-api rolled back, and "version":"1.1.0" again.

checks.text: Every object applies and the API rolls out in the shop namespace.
The service answers through the NodePort and uses its Redis cache.
With Redis stopped, the API Pods are Running but not ready.
The new ConfigMap value reaches the Pods only after the restart.
The autoscaler scales the Deployment out under load and back in afterwards.
The rolling update reaches 1.2.0 and the rollback restores 1.1.0.

lab.submit: Paste the commands and output from steps 3 to 6 and 9 to 11; for the watches, include the lines where the replica count changes.

files.content:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: redis
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    app: redis
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redis
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: redis
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: redis
          image: redis:8.2-alpine
          args: ["redis-server", "--requirepass", "$(REDIS_PASSWORD)"]
          env:
            - name: REDIS_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: redis-auth
                  key: password
          ports:
            - name: redis
              containerPort: 6379
          readinessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["sh", "-c", "redis-cli -a \"$REDIS_PASSWORD\" --no-auth-warning ping | grep -q PONG"]
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              memory: 128Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: redis
  namespace: shop
spec:
  selector:
    app: redis
  ports:
    - name: redis
      port: 6379
      targetPort: redis

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: inventory-config
  namespace: shop
data:
  REDIS_HOST: redis
  REDIS_PORT: "6379"
  CACHE_TTL_SECONDS: "30"

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: inventory-api
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    app: inventory-api
spec:
  # No replicas field: the HorizontalPodAutoscaler in 50-hpa.yaml owns the count.
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: inventory-api
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: inventory-api
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: inventory-api:1.1.0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8000
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: inventory-config
          env:
            - name: REDIS_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: redis-auth
                  key: password
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 15
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 96Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 192Mi
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: inventory-api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: inventory-api
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
      nodePort: 30080

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: inventory-api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: inventory-api
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 6
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 60

hints: API Pods stuck in CreateContainerConfigError mean the redis-auth Secret is missing: create it (step 2) and they start by themselves.
If kubectl top says metrics aren't available, give metrics-server a minute; kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/metrics-server shows certificate errors if the argument didn't take effect.
TARGETS showing <unknown> means the autoscaler has no metrics yet, or the Pods have no CPU request.
On Windows, run these commands in Git Bash or WSL; PowerShell quotes the JSON in step 6 differently. If python3 isn't found, use python.

modules.title: Managing K8s Clusters
modules.summary: Use kubectl to inspect, diagnose and fix workloads, expose services with Ingress, share a cluster fairly with quotas and limits, and keep applications available while nodes are drained and upgraded.

lessons.title: kubectl for operators: contexts, output and inspection
objectives: Point kubectl at the right cluster and namespace
Inspect objects, events and logs to understand what a workload is doing
key_points: kubectl reads clusters, users and contexts from a kubeconfig file (~/.kube/config, or the files in KUBECONFIG). kubectl config get-contexts lists them and use-context switches, so check where you're pointed before changing anything.

kubectl get lists objects: -o wide adds nodes and IP addresses, -o yaml shows the whole object, -l filters by label, -A covers every namespace, -w watches for changes, and -o jsonpath or custom-columns picks out fields for scripts.
kubectl describe shows an object's details and its recent events, which usually state a problem's cause; kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp lists a namespace's events in time order.

kubectl logs shows a container's output (-f to follow, --previous for the last crashed run, -c to choose a container); kubectl exec runs a command in a container, and kubectl port-forward connects a local port to a Pod or Service for testing.
kubectl debug adds an ephemeral container with your choice of tools to a running Pod, which helps when the application's image has no shell.

walkthrough.title: Inspect a workload from the outside in

steps.do: Check which cluster and namespace you're about to work on.
steps.code:
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config current-context

steps.do: Get an overview of a namespace, then one Pod in full.
steps.code:
kubectl -n shop get all -o wide
kubectl -n shop get pod $(kubectl -n shop get pods -l app=inventory-api -o name | head -n 1 | cut -d/ -f2) -o yaml | head -n 40

steps.do: Pick out fields for a report: every Pod's name, node and restart count.
steps.code: kubectl -n shop get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount

steps.do: Read the namespace's events in order.
steps.code: kubectl -n shop get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 10

steps.do: Follow the logs of every API Pod at once, prefixed with the Pod name (Ctrl+C to stop).
steps.code: kubectl -n shop logs -l app=inventory-api -f --prefix

steps.do: The API image has a shell, but many don't: attach a debugging container that shares the API container's process namespace.
steps.code: kubectl -n shop debug -it deploy/inventory-api --image=busybox:1.37 --target=api -- sh
steps.see: A busybox prompt; ps shows uvicorn running in the API container. Type exit to leave.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Pods that won't run or won't serve
objectives: Diagnose the common failure states from their symptoms
Follow a repeatable path from symptom to root cause
key_points: Pending means the scheduler can't place the Pod; describe says why, such as insufficient CPU or memory, a taint it doesn't tolerate, or a PersistentVolumeClaim that isn't bound.

ErrImagePull and then ImagePullBackOff mean the image can't be pulled: a wrong name or tag, a registry that needs credentials (imagePullSecrets) or, on kind, an image never loaded; Kubernetes keeps retrying with growing delays.

CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps starting and exiting. Read kubectl logs --previous for the error, and look for OOMKilled under Last State in describe, which means the memory limit is too low.
CreateContainerConfigError means a referenced ConfigMap, Secret or key is missing. A Pod that is Running but not ready has a failing readiness probe, and its events say what the probe got back.

A Service that doesn't answer usually has no endpoints: compare its selector with the Pods' labels (kubectl get pods --show-labels) and check its EndpointSlices, then test from a temporary Pod inside the cluster before suspecting the network.

lessons.title: Ingress, quotas and limits
objectives: Expose HTTP services through an Ingress controller, and describe Gateway API
Share a namespace fairly with ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges
key_points: An Ingress (networking.k8s.io/v1) routes outside HTTP and HTTPS traffic to Services by host name and path, with TLS certificates from Secrets. It does nothing until an Ingress controller runs in the cluster, chosen with ingressClassName.

Many controllers implement Ingress, such as Traefik, HAProxy, Contour and those from cloud providers. The community Ingress NGINX controller stopped receiving updates, security fixes included, in March 2026, so choose a maintained controller.

The Ingress API is stable but frozen. Gateway API (gateway.networking.k8s.io) is its successor: it splits the job between GatewayClass, Gateway and route objects such as HTTPRoute, and builds in features such as weighted traffic splitting.

A ResourceQuota caps a namespace's totals, such as its number of Pods or the sum of its CPU and memory requests and limits. Once a quota covers CPU or memory, every new Pod there must set them, or it's rejected.
A LimitRange gives containers that don't set requests and limits default values, and can set a minimum and maximum per container, so a quota doesn't reject Pods that forgot them.

lessons.title: Keeping applications available during maintenance
objectives: Drain nodes safely with PodDisruptionBudgets in place
Spread replicas so the loss of a node doesn't take a service down
key_points: kubectl cordon marks a node unschedulable; kubectl drain cordons it and evicts its Pods so their controllers recreate them elsewhere (add --ignore-daemonsets, and --delete-emptydir-data for Pods with emptyDir volumes); kubectl uncordon brings it back.

A PodDisruptionBudget (policy/v1) limits voluntary disruptions such as drains: with minAvailable: 2, an eviction that would leave fewer than two ready Pods is refused until a replacement is ready somewhere else.

Replicas only protect you if they run on different nodes: topologySpreadConstraints, or pod anti-affinity, spread a Deployment's Pods using node labels such as kubernetes.io/hostname and topology.kubernetes.io/zone.
With whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule, a spread rule can leave Pods Pending when there are too few nodes, for example during a drain; ScheduleAnyway treats the spread as a preference instead.

PodDisruptionBudgets don't stop involuntary disruptions such as a node failing; spread replicas and readiness probes are what keep a service up then. Upgrade clusters one minor version at a time, control plane first, then nodes, and keep kubectl within one minor version of the API server.

lab.title: Troubleshoot a broken namespace
lab.goal: Find and fix five broken workloads with get, describe, logs and events, watch a ResourceQuota stop a scale-up, and send traffic to a repaired service through an Ingress controller.
setup: The kind cluster from the earlier labs, with inventory-api:1.1.0 loaded
Helm, for installing the Traefik Ingress controller
Download the starter files into a folder called debug

steps.do: Create the namespace with its quota and default limits, then the workloads.
steps.code:
kubectl apply -f debug/00-namespace.yaml
kubectl apply -f debug/
kubectl -n debug get deployments,pods
steps.see: Five Deployments, most of them not ready, and Pods in several different states.

steps.do: Start broad: list the Pods and the recent events, then describe the orders Pod.
steps.code:
kubectl -n debug get pods
kubectl -n debug get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 20
kubectl -n debug describe pod -l app=orders | tail -n 15
steps.see: ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff for orders, CreateContainerConfigError for stock, 0/1 ready for pricing and CrashLoopBackOff for reports.

steps.do: Look closer at stock, reports and pricing.
steps.code:
kubectl -n debug describe pod -l app=stock | grep -i 'error'
kubectl -n debug describe pod -l app=reports | grep -A 4 'Last State'
kubectl -n debug describe pod -l app=pricing | grep -i 'readiness probe failed'
steps.see: A missing key in ConfigMap stock-config, Reason: OOMKilled, and HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 404.

steps.do: The catalogue Pod is healthy, yet its Service doesn't answer. Compare the Service's selector with the Pod's labels, and look at its endpoints.
steps.code:
kubectl -n debug get pods --show-labels
kubectl -n debug get service catalogue -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'; echo
kubectl -n debug get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=catalogue
steps.see: The Pod is labelled app=catalogue, the Service selects {"app":"catalog"}, and its EndpointSlice has no endpoints.

steps.do: Fix the manifests: the image tag in 01 (1.1.0), the ConfigMap key in 02, the probe path in 03 (the app serves /healthz), the memory request and limit in 04 (128Mi) and the selector in 05. Apply them and check.
steps.code:
kubectl apply -f debug/
kubectl -n debug get pods
steps.see: All five Pods Running and 1/1 ready after a minute or so.

steps.do: See the quota at work: ask for 8 catalogue replicas, more than the namespace's 10 Pods allow, then scale back.
steps.code:
kubectl -n debug scale deployment catalogue --replicas=8
sleep 5
kubectl -n debug describe resourcequota debug-quota
kubectl -n debug get events --field-selector reason=FailedCreate | tail -n 3
kubectl -n debug scale deployment catalogue --replicas=1
steps.see: pods 10 of 10 used, and FailedCreate events that say exceeded quota: debug-quota.

steps.do: Install Traefik as the Ingress controller, then check its IngressClass and the Ingress from 06-ingress.yaml.
steps.code:
helm repo add traefik https://traefik.github.io/charts
helm install traefik traefik/traefik -n traefik --create-namespace
kubectl get ingressclass
kubectl -n debug get ingress catalogue
steps.see: An IngressClass called traefik, and the catalogue Ingress for host catalogue.local.

steps.do: Forward a local port to Traefik once its Pod is running, and send a request with the Ingress's host name.
steps.code:
kubectl -n traefik rollout status deployment/traefik
kubectl -n traefik port-forward svc/traefik 8080:80 &
sleep 3
curl -s -H 'Host: catalogue.local' http://localhost:8080/
kill %1
steps.see: {"service":"inventory-api","version":"1.1.0",...}, served through the Ingress.

steps.do: Write a short incident note for each of the five problems: the symptom, the command that showed the cause, the cause, and the fix.

checks.text: The image problem is diagnosed and fixed.
The missing ConfigMap key is diagnosed and fixed.
The failing readiness probe and the low memory limit are diagnosed and fixed.
The Service's selector mismatch is found and fixed.
The quota stops the scale-up.
Requests reach the repaired service through the Ingress, and the incident notes cover all five problems.

lab.submit: Paste the commands and output from steps 2 to 8, then your five incident notes.

files.content:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: debug
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: debug-quota
  namespace: debug
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "10"
    requests.cpu: "1"
    requests.memory: 1Gi
    limits.cpu: "3"
    limits.memory: 2Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: debug-defaults
  namespace: debug
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 50m
        memory: 64Mi
      default:
        cpu: 250m
        memory: 128Mi

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: debug
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: inventory-api:1.1
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: stock-config
  namespace: debug
data:
  CACHE_TTL_SECONDS: "60"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: stock
  namespace: debug
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: stock
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: stock
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: inventory-api:1.1.0
          env:
            - name: CACHE_TTL_SECONDS
              valueFrom:
                configMapKeyRef:
                  name: stock-config
                  key: cache-ttl
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: pricing
  namespace: debug
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: pricing
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: pricing
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: inventory-api:1.1.0
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8000
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: reports
  namespace: debug
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: reports
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: reports
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: inventory-api:1.1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: 20Mi
            limits:
              memory: 20Mi

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: catalogue
  namespace: debug
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: catalogue
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: catalogue
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: inventory-api:1.1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: catalogue
  namespace: debug
spec:
  selector:
    app: catalog
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8000

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: catalogue
  namespace: debug
spec:
  ingressClassName: traefik
  rules:
    - host: catalogue.local
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: catalogue
                port:
                  number: 80

hints: describe ends with Events, which usually state the cause in plain words: read them before anything else.
logs --previous shows the last crashed container's output; without it you see the current attempt, which may not have printed anything yet. A container killed for memory may print nothing at all.
If a fixed Deployment still shows a failing Pod, it's the old one on its way out: kubectl -n debug rollout status deployment/NAME waits for the new one.
If port-forward says the port is in use, choose another local port, such as 8081:80, and use it in curl.

study_plan.focus: Learn how containers isolate processes, practise the container lifecycle and write a first Dockerfile for inventory-api.
Rebuild the image as a lean multi-stage build and run the API with Redis under Docker Compose.
Learn Kubernetes' architecture and core objects, and explore them on a three-node kind cluster.
Deploy the service from manifests with probes, configuration, secrets and autoscaling, and practise a rolling update and a rollback.
Troubleshoot broken workloads, add Ingress and quotas, build the capstone, and review with the mock exam and flashcards.

project.title: Ship a highly available inventory service
project.brief: Take inventory-api from a developer's laptop to a small but production-shaped Kubernetes deployment. Package it with a lean, multi-stage Dockerfile that runs as a non-root user, and give developers a compose.yaml that runs the API and Redis with healthchecks, a private network and a persistent volume. Then write numbered Kubernetes manifests for a three-node kind (or minikube) cluster: a namespace with a ResourceQuota and a LimitRange; Redis as a StatefulSet (or a Deployment with the Recreate strategy) with its data on a PersistentVolumeClaim and its password in a Secret created outside Git; the API with at least three replicas spread across nodes, startup, readiness and liveness probes, requests and limits, settings from a ConfigMap, a PodDisruptionBudget and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler; and access from your computer through a NodePort or an Ingress. Prove it works with the smoke test, keep it serving while you delete an API Pod and drain a worker node that isn't running Redis, and document how to run and operate it.
deliverables: Dockerfile, .dockerignore and compose.yaml, with docker compose ps output showing both services healthy
A k8s folder of numbered manifests for every object listed in the brief
The output of kubectl get all,pvc,pdb,hpa -n shop -o wide, showing the API's Pods on different nodes
The output of python smoke_test.py http://localhost:30080 (or your Ingress address) with all 4 checks passed
An availability test: the output of smoke_test.py --watch 120 while you delete an API Pod and drain a worker, with the kubectl commands you ran
README.md: how to run the service with Compose and on kind, how settings and the password are supplied, and a short troubleshooting guide

rubric.name: Container images
rubric.description: A multi-stage Dockerfile with a slim runtime stage, a numeric non-root user, an exec-form CMD, pinned base images, a cache-friendly layer order and a .dockerignore; no secrets in any layer.

rubric.name: Local development with Compose
rubric.description: Both services start healthy and in the right order, on a private network, with Redis data in a named volume; docker compose config validates the file.

rubric.name: Kubernetes manifests
rubric.description: Valid, numbered manifests with the right API versions, consistent labels and selectors, probes that separate readiness from liveness, requests and limits, settings from a ConfigMap and the password from a Secret.

rubric.name: High availability and scaling
rubric.description: At least three API replicas spread across nodes, a PodDisruptionBudget that lets the drain finish without an outage, a working autoscaler, and a watch test with no failed requests, or a clear explanation of any.

rubric.name: Storage, quotas and access
rubric.description: Redis on a PersistentVolumeClaim, a ResourceQuota and LimitRange in the namespace, and a NodePort or Ingress that works from the host.

rubric.name: Evidence and documentation
rubric.description: The outputs prove each claim, and the README lets a colleague run and troubleshoot the service and understand the main design decisions.

project.submit: Paste your Dockerfile, compose.yaml, every manifest and README.md, then the outputs listed in the deliverables.

files.content:
"""Smoke-test a deployed inventory-api: python smoke_test.py http://localhost:30080

With --watch SECONDS it instead calls the service twice a second for that long and counts failures,
which shows whether it stays up while you delete Pods or drain a node.
Uses only the Python standard library.
"""

import argparse
import json
import sys
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request


def call(base, path, method="GET"):
    req = urllib.request.Request(base + path, method=method)
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as resp:  # a new connection each time
        return resp.status, json.loads(resp.read())


def checks(base):
    passed = 0
    status, body = call(base, "/")
    ok = status == 200 and body.get("service") == "inventory-api"
    print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'} service: {body.get('service')} {body.get('version')}")
    passed += ok

    try:
        status, body = call(base, "/readyz")
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        status, body = e.code, {"status": "not ready"}
    ok = status == 200
    print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'} readiness: {body.get('status')}")
    passed += ok

    call(base, "/items/sku-1002")
    _, second = call(base, "/items/sku-1002")
    ok = second.get("cache") == "hit"
    print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'} cache: second lookup was a {second.get('cache')}")
    passed += ok

    counts, hosts = [], set()
    try:
        for _ in range(12):
            _, body = call(base, "/visits", method="POST")
            counts.append(body["visits"])
            hosts.add(body["host"])
        ok = all(b > a for a, b in zip(counts, counts[1:]))
        print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'} shared state: visits rose from {counts[0]} to {counts[-1]} "
              f"across {len(hosts)} pod(s)")
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        ok = False
        print(f"FAIL shared state: POST /visits returned {e.code}")
    passed += ok

    print(f"{'All' if passed == 4 else 'Only'} {passed} of 4 checks passed")
    return passed == 4


def watch(base, seconds):
    total = failed = 0
    hosts = set()
    end = time.monotonic() + seconds
    while time.monotonic() < end:
        total += 1
        try:
            _, body = call(base, "/")
            hosts.add(body["host"])
        except (urllib.error.URLError, OSError):
            failed += 1
        time.sleep(0.5)
    print(f"{total} requests, {failed} failed, answered by {len(hosts)} pod(s)")
    return failed == 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("base_url", help="for example http://localhost:30080")
    parser.add_argument("--watch", type=int, metavar="SECONDS", help="keep calling the service for this long")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    base = args.base_url.rstrip("/")
    ok = watch(base, args.watch) if args.watch else checks(base)
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
